'''Karen Elizabeth Wetterhahn''' (October 16, 1948 – June 8, 1997), also known as '''Karen Wetterhahn Jennette''',<ref name=lippard/> was an American professor of [[chemistry]] at [[Dartmouth College]] in [[Hanover, New Hampshire]], who specialized in toxic metal exposure. She died of [[mercury poisoning]] at the age of 48 due to accidental exposure to the extremely toxic organic [[mercury (element)|mercury]] compound [[dimethylmercury]] ({{chem2|Hg(CH3)2}}). Protective gloves in use at the time of the incident provided insufficient protection, and exposure to only one or two drops of the dimethylmercury absorbed through the gloves proved to be fatal after less than a year.

==Career==

Wetterhahn was born in [[Plattsburgh, New York]].<ref name=LATimes>{{cite news |title=Karen Wetterhahn; Dartmouth Scientist |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |date=June 12, 1997 |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-06-12-mn-2765-story.html |access-date=July 11, 2014 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714235213/http://articles.latimes.com/1997-06-12/news/mn-2765_1_karen-wetterhahn |archive-date=July 14, 2014}}</ref> She earned her bachelor's degree from [[St. Lawrence University|St.{{nbs}}Lawrence University]] in 1970 and her [[doctorate]] from [[Columbia University]] in 1975.<ref>{{cite journal |title=In Memoriam Karen E. Wetterhahn, Ph.D. 1948−1997 |journal=[[Chemical Research in Toxicology]] |date=1997 |volume=10 |issue=9 |page=923 |doi=10.1021/tx9704922|doi-access=free }}</ref> Her doctoral work was supervised by [[Stephen J. Lippard]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Long |first1=Janice |title=Mercury poisoning fatal to chemist |journal=[[Chemical & Engineering News]] |date=1997 |volume=75 |issue=24 |pages=11–12 |doi=10.1021/cen-v075n024.p011a}}</ref> She joined Dartmouth's faculty in 1976 as their first female chemistry professor and published more than 85 research papers.<ref name=LATimes/><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Blayney |first=Michael B. |last2=Nierenberg |first2=David |last3=O’Halloran |first3=Thomas V. |last4=Wilcox |first4=Dean E. |last5=Winn |first5=John S. |date=2022-06-08 |title=Twenty-Five Years Ago&#xe5f8;Remembering the Life and Loss of Professor Karen E. Wetterhahn |url=https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chas.2c00034 |journal=ACS Chemical Health & Safety |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=325–326 |doi=10.1021/acs.chas.2c00034  |doi-access=free|issn=2472-1115}}</ref> In 1990, Wetterhahn helped establish Dartmouth College's Women in Science Project (WISP), which helped to raise the share of women science majors from 13 to 25 percent at Dartmouth College and has become a national model.<ref name=LATimes/><ref name=treling>{{cite news |title=The Trembling Edge of Science |last=Endicott |first=Karen |newspaper=Dartmouth Alumni Magazine |date=April 1998 |url=https://archive.dartmouthalumnimagazine.com/article/1998/4/1/the-trembling-edge-of-science |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140715003519/http://stemed.unm.edu/PDFs/cd/CLASSROOM_LAB_SAFETY/Trembling_Edge_Science.pdf |archive-date=2014-07-15}}</ref><ref name=tribute>{{cite web |title=A Tribute to Karen Wetterhahn |publisher=Dartmouth College |date=May 1, 2009 |url=https://sites.dartmouth.edu/toxmetal/about-us/a-tribute-to-karen-wetterhahn/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090626070531/http://www.dartmouth.edu/~toxmetal/home/tribute/karen.html |archive-date=June 26, 2009}}</ref>

== Research ==
Wetterhahn's research primarily focused on the toxic effects of metals on living organisms, with particular interest in [[hexavalent chromium]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Standeven |first=Andrew M. |last2=Wetterhahn |first2=Karen E. |date=1989-12-01 |title=Chromium(VI) Toxicity: Uptake, Reduction, and DNA Damage |url=https://doi.org/10.3109/10915818909009118 |journal=Journal of the American College of Toxicology |language=EN |publisher=SAGE Publications |volume=8 |issue=7 |pages=1275–1283 |doi=10.3109/10915818909009118 |issn=0730-0913}}</ref>

==Accident and death==

On August 14, 1996, Wetterhahn, a specialist in toxic metal exposure, was studying how [[mercury (element)|mercury]] [[ion|ions]] interact with [[DNA repair]] proteins and investigating the toxic properties of another highly toxic [[heavy metal (chemistry)|heavy metal]], [[cadmium]]. She was using [[dimethylmercury]], at the time the standard [[chemical shift#Chemical shift referencing|internal reference]] for {{chem2|^{199}Hg}} [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] (NMR) measurements.<ref name=story>{{cite journal |last=Cotton |first=Simon |title=Dimethylmercury and Mercury Poisoning: The Karen Wetterhahn story |website=Molecule of the Month |publisher=[[Bristol University]] School of Chemistry |doi=10.6084/m9.figshare.5245807 |date=October 2003 |url=https://www.chm.bris.ac.uk/motm/dimethylmercury/dmmh.htm |access-date=January 6, 2021 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120530061417/http://www.chm.bris.ac.uk/motm/dimethylmercury/dmmh.htm |archive-date=May 30, 2012}}</ref>

Wetterhahn later recalled that she had spilled several drops of dimethylmercury from the tip of a pipette onto her latex-gloved hand.<ref name=nejm/> Not believing herself in any immediate danger, as she was taking all recommended precautions,<ref name=natgeo/> she proceeded to clean up the area prior to removing her protective clothing.<ref name=nejm>{{cite journal |last1=Nierenberg |first1=David W. |last2=Nordgren |first2=Richard E. |last3=Chang |first3=Morris B. |last4=Siegler |first4=Richard W. |last5=Blayney |first5=Michael B. |last6=Hochberg |first6=Fred |last7=Toribara |first7=Taft Y. |last8=Cernichiari |first8=Elsa |last9=Clarkson |first9=Thomas |title=Delayed Cerebellar Disease and Death after Accidental Exposure to Dimethylmercury |journal=[[New England Journal of Medicine]] |volume=338 |issue=23 |year=1998 |pages=1672–1676 |pmid=9614258 |doi=10.1056/NEJM199806043382305|doi-access=free }}</ref> However, tests later revealed that dimethylmercury can, in fact, rapidly permeate several kinds of latex gloves and enter the skin within about 15 seconds.<ref name=story/> Her exposure was later confirmed by [[hair analysis]], which showed a dramatic jump in mercury levels 17 days after the initial accident, peaking at 39 days, followed by a gradual decline.<ref name=nejm/>

Approximately three months after the initial accident, Wetterhahn began experiencing brief episodes of abdominal discomfort and noticed significant weight loss. The more distinctive neurological symptoms of mercury poisoning, including loss of balance and slurred speech, appeared in January 1997, five months after the accident.<ref name=nejm/> At that point, tests proved that she had severe [[mercury poisoning]].<ref name=treling/><ref name=tribute/><ref name=natgeo>{{cite magazine |last=Newman |first=Cathy |title=Pick Your Poison – 12 Toxic Tales |magazine=[[National Geographic]] |date=May 2005 |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/poison-toxic-tales |access-date=2009-03-07 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090218234139/http://science.nationalgeographic.com/science/health-and-human-body/human-body/poison-toxic-tales.html |archive-date=2009-02-18}}</ref> Her blood and urinary mercury content were measured at 4,000&nbsp;μg/L<ref name=story/> and 234&nbsp;μg/L, respectively—both many times their respective toxic thresholds of 200&nbsp;μg/L and 50&nbsp;μg/L (blood and urine reference ranges are 1 to 8&nbsp;μg/L and 1 to 5&nbsp;μg/L).<ref name=nejm/>

Despite aggressive [[chelation therapy]], her condition rapidly deteriorated. Three weeks after the first neurological symptoms appeared, Wetterhahn lapsed into what appeared to be a vegetative state punctuated by periods of extreme agitation.<ref name=nejm/> One of her former students said, "Her husband saw tears rolling down her face. I asked if she was in pain. The doctors said it didn't appear that her brain could even register pain."<ref name=natgeo/> Wetterhahn was removed from [[life support]] and pronounced dead on June 8, 1997, ten months after her initial exposure.<ref name=nejm/>

The case proved that the standard precautions at the time, all of which Wetterhahn had carefully followed, were inadequate for "super-toxic" chemicals like dimethylmercury.<ref name=nejm/> In response, the [[Occupational Safety and Health Administration]] (OSHA) recommended that the use of dimethylmercury be avoided unless absolutely necessary and mandated the use of plastic-laminate gloves when handling this compound.<ref name=OSHA>{{cite web |publisher=Office of Science and Technology Assessment, [[Occupational Safety and Health Administration]] |website=OSHA Hazard Information Bulletins |title=Dimethylmercury |last=Witt |first=Steven F. |date=March 9, 1998 |url=https://www.osha.gov/publications/hib19980309 |access-date=March 22, 2021}}</ref> Her death prompted consideration of using an alternative reference material for mercury [[nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy|NMR spectroscopy]] experiments.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Zacks |first=Rebecca |title=Looking for alternatives |magazine=[[Scientific American]] |volume=277 |issue=3 |page=20 |date=September 1997}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Blayney |first1=Michael B. |last2=Winn |first2=John S. |last3=Nierenberg |first3=David W. |title=Handling dimethylmercury |magazine=[[Chemical & Engineering News]] |volume=75 |issue=19 |page=7 |doi=10.1021/cen-v075n019.p007 |date=May 12, 1997 |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/cen-v075n019.p007}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Toriba |first1=Taft Y. |last2=Clarkson |first2=Thomas W. |last3=Nierenberg |first3=David W. |title=More on working with dimethylmercury |magazine=[[Chemical and Engineering News]] |volume=75 |issue=24 |page=6 |doi=10.1021/cen-v075n024.p006 |date=June 16, 1997 |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/cen-v075n024.p006}}</ref>

==Legacy==
Wetterhahn's accidental exposure occurred despite her having taken all measures required at that time. These included the use of [[latex gloves]], a [[fume hood]], and adherence to standard safety procedures. After Wetterhahn's [[mercury poisoning]] was discovered, her colleagues tested various safety gloves against dimethylmercury and found that the small, [[apolar]] molecule diffuses through most of them in seconds, much more quickly than expected.<ref name=story/><ref name=nejm/> As a result, it is now recommended by OSHA to wear laminate gloves, which should be worn under an outer glove that is resistant to abrasion and tears, while handling dimethylmercury.

At the time, dimethylmercury was the common calibration standard for {{chem2|^{199}Hg}} [[nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy|NMR spectroscopy]] because it has certain advantages over other alternatives.<ref name=ohalloran>{{cite web |title=<sup>199</sup>Hg NMR Standards |last1=O'Halloran |first1=Thomas V. |last2=Singer |first2=Christopher P. |publisher=Northwestern University |date=March 10, 1998 |url=https://sites.northwestern.edu/ohalloran/199hg-nmr-standards/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130603111937/http://chemgroups.northwestern.edu/ohalloran/HgNMRStandards/ |archive-date=June 3, 2013}}</ref> As a consequence of Wetterhahn's accident, safety recommendations have been revised, and the use of dimethylmercury for any purpose has been highly discouraged.<ref name=OSHA/> Wetterhahn's legacy includes a significant and lasting improvement in laboratory safety.<ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=[[Chemistry World]] |last=Cavanaugh |first=Ray |title=The dangers of dimethylmercury |publisher=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]] |date=February 2019 |url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/opinion/the-dangers-of-dimethylmercury-/3010064.article |access-date=January 6, 2021}}</ref>

Dartmouth College has since established an award in Wetterhahn's name (The Karen E. Wetterhahn Graduate Fellowship in Chemistry, created in 1998 and funded by the Karen E. Wetterhahn Memorial Fund) to encourage other women to pursue careers in science. It is a one-year fellowship given to an exceptionally good chemistry graduate student who will receive their PhD within two years. Whenever possible, a woman is preferred for the award.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Karen E. Wetterhahn Graduate Fellowship in Chemistry |publisher=Dartmouth College |date=January 30, 2014 |url=https://chemistry.dartmouth.edu/graduate/graduate-awards/karen-e-wetterhahn-graduate-fellowship-chemistry |access-date=July 15, 2014 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150710203132/http://chemistry.dartmouth.edu/graduate/graduate-awards/karen-e-wetterhahn-graduate-fellowship-chemistry |archive-date=July 10, 2015}}</ref> The [[National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences]] also maintains the Karen Wetterhahn Memorial Award, awarded annually to a graduate student or post-doctoral researcher.<ref>{{cite web |title=Karen Wetterhahn Memorial Award |publisher=[[National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences]] |date=June 27, 2013 |url=https://www.niehs.nih.gov/research/supported/centers/srp/training/wetterhahn |access-date=July 14, 2014 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120814093437/http://www.niehs.nih.gov/research/supported/srp/training/wetterhahn/ |archive-date=August 14, 2012}}</ref>
